title: Price an at-the-money option with four numbers, then use realized vol
summary: An at-the-money option is worth about 0.4 x stock price x volatility x the square root of days over 360. With a $100 stock, 25% IV and 30 days, that is about $2.87. Put realized volatility, say 10%, in place of IV and the fair value is about $1.15, so the market pays about $1.72 of volatility premium. If realized is above implied, it is a poor sell.

params.label: Excess drift over rate
params.help: Your view of annual return above the risk-free rate. Zero = the market view; EV is then about zero.

steps.caption: The stock is $100 and we price the $100 call, 30 days out.
The market's distribution at 25% implied volatility.
The one-sigma move: about 0.25 x sqrt(30/360) of the price, close to $7.
Rule of thumb: 0.4 x 100 x 0.25 x sqrt(30/360) gives about $2.87 for the option.
Priced with 10% realized vol it is worth about $1.15. The $1.72 gap is the premium the seller collects.
Set IV to 10% to see the narrower distribution that realized volatility implies.

takeaways: An ATM option is worth about 0.4 x price x vol x sqrt(days/360).
The rule only works near the money.
Price the option with realized vol to estimate fair value.
Sell when implied is well above realized; avoid selling when realized is above implied.
caveats: The speaker's VAY Chrome extension and screener are promotional and not verified here.
He uses 360 days in the formula; the exact convention changes the answer slightly.
